Marriage isn't really about finding the most compatible person. That's a very modern misconception.

Why? Because we change over time. The experiences and years of our lives transform us into different people.

Even if you could find a perfectly compatible person, over the years you would both change in different ways.

Don't try to find the person that is most compatible with you. My advice is to choose a spouse on 2 criteria: great friend, great character. 

No matter how each of you change along the way, friendship and character will hold you together. Next year is my 24th year anniversary. My wife are very different people, but I can't imagine doing life without her.

I think Tim Keller put it best in The Meaning of Marriage

Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

This concept from Byung-Chul Han will rewire your brain:

"Attentional fasting"

Normal fasting, by starving you, forces your cells to consume their own worn-out parts and junk proteins. This scarcity-induced "clearing house" process makes the organism stronger.

Similarly, "attentional fasting" is when you take away external stimulation and force your brain to stimulate ITSELF with its previously acquired set of memories, experiences, and ideas. In this process, you:

- cast out mental debris

- digest events which were previously only half-chewed

- recombine disparate memories into a coherent Life Story

Before 24/7 algorithmic "for-you" pages, humans were "attention fasting" for long stretches of time. Their minds, deprived of stimulation, turned inward to look for it...and in the process, unlocked a deeper layer of neurochemical cohesion. A "clearing house" process induced by boredom. Byung-Chul Han calls this process "the autophagy of the soul," autophagy being the process via which the cells turn inward for energy and consume their own damaged elements.

The internet led to a total extinction of boredom, and that's why we have no attentional fasting today. Your mind is overfed with stimulating media to the point where it completely loses the ability (and the desire) to look inward. It turns out that when boredom dies, so does self-reflection. And when self-reflection dies, so does the self.

The environment is NOT destiny, though. Free-will is real. While the "attentional fasts" that were naturally embedded into daily life are now gone, we can bring them back by purposefully and ritualistically cutting our own access to the firehose of contextless stimulation that is the internet.

Thank you for reading. I appreciate your "attention" ;)

My brutally honest advice to someone who wants to make a lot of money.

3 things nobody told you:

1. The only way to make a lot of money is to create a lot of value.

No one hands out money. No one is going to pay you just because they like you or think you're cool.

Money earned is a direct byproduct of value created.

The only way to get rich is to create an enormous amount of value for others, and capture a small portion of that along the way.

You create value by doing three things:

- Identify problems
- Create solutions
- Scale those solutions

It's not talking about the thing, it's not brainstorming about the thing, it's not asking about the thing, it's not thinking about the thing. The only way to create value is by doing the thing.

And if you don't know where to start, look around you. Customers, colleagues, bosses, shareholders, employees. Every single one of them has a problem.

What problems can you solve for the people around you?

Figure them out, solve them, scale that solution.

That's how you make money.

2. You don't need passion, you need energy.

I still have no idea what it means to follow your passion.

You don't have to be passionate about your professional pursuits, you just need to find energy in them. You just need to feel a pull towards them. You just need to feel that spark of curiosity in them.

Passion is usually a byproduct of energy.

When you have energy for something, you'll give it your deep attention to learn more.

You’ll ask the right questions. You’ll figure it out. You’ll win.

Follow your energy. Pursue interesting puzzles. Solve them.

3. You have to demonstrate excellence in everything you do.

Your income scales proportional to the amount of excellence that you're able to demonstrate.

Strategic incompetence is a lie. You don't get to pick and choose when to show up, because the world will ignore your best and judge you for your worst. Everything matters. Every single thing.

Top performers show up with energy and enthusiasm for the little things just as much as they do for the big things.

If you're in the top-10% of performers, there's no ceiling for what you can do. But the self-awareness to identify where you currently stack up, and adapt to the honest feedback on it, is very rare.

If you're in the top-10%, you know it. If you're not, figure out why and fix it.

Before Hollywood, I was living in a van in Hawaii and waiting tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp Company. One day, the incredible Rae Dawn Chong walked into the restaurant, and naturally, I went up to her table and said, “Hey, you’re a movie star! What are you doing here?”

She asked if I could act, and I said, “Fuck yeah, put me in your movie!”

She asked for my phone number. The only problem was I didn’t have one. So I gave her my buddy Mike’s number instead. A couple days later, Mike casually mentions, “Oh, by the way, someone called you.” ARE YOU KIDDING ME, MIKE?!

I called her back, and sure enough, she was serious. I drove over to pick up the script, went back to Mike’s house, and read all 120 pages three times in a row. First script I’d ever read. My character's name was Devon, and I remember thinking, “Sweet! I could totally play a Devon!”

I showed up to the audition with every line and inflection mapped out in pencil. Rae told me I could act and offered me the part. I asked if we were shooting in Hawaii. Nope. Los Angeles.

I had about $60 to my name, a bag of clothes, and some rollerblades.

Then Rae told me they'd fly me out. And I remember thinking right then and there, my life just changed forever. I'm going to be an actor.

That little movie was Cursed Part 3, a low-budget horror comedy that opened the door to Hollywood for me.

I'll forever be grateful to Rae for taking a chance on a kid working at a shrimp restaurant. Everybody starts somewhere, and this is where it all began for me.

I think ambitious people should treat life in “seasons” rather than trying to balance everything every day.

A few years massively overallocated to work. A period getting seriously fit. A year or two nomading. Then family takes priority for a while. Then maybe at 35 you go completely insane again and spend four years building a new company, and so on.

The mistake is thinking every metric needs to stay green all the time. Most great outcomes (building a company, writing sth serious, training for an event) need uninterrupted runs, not daily moderation. Sometimes work should suffer cause you’re travelling, sometimes your social life should suffer cause you’re building, sometimes career progression should slow cause family matters more. That’s fine.

And tbh it probably makes life more fun too. You get actual chapters and completely different versions of yourself instead of spending 40 years maintaining the same perfectly optimised routine. A few intense years in one city, a weird nomad phase, an obsession that takes over your life, then something completely different. Probably much more memorable than one very long well-optimised Tuesday.

It's why I encourage everyone to think of balance in years, not days. A good life can look horribly unbalanced on some random Tuesday and still be very balanced over 10 years.

one of my strongest lived experiences and biggest lessons over the last two years: 

every struggling phase, personally or professionally, should have either of these two things: a defined outcome (i want to get to x, no matter how long it takes), or a defined timeline (i want to end this struggling phase for a greater purpose i can achieve in x months). 

the most ideal case is to have both, a timeline bound outcome, which gives you two things: something to look forward to, and the momentum that makes the struggle worth it.

when you have neither, no defined outcome and no timeline, you just loop over the same problems and the struggle starts to feel meaningless. the way out is simple: define at least one of the two.

not to say that once you're outcome or timeline bound, the struggle ends. you just earn the privilege to solve different, better, more aligned to yourself kinds of problems as you grow, which is what i'd like to believe we're all optimizing for.

The world wants me to die.  

My incurable disease diagnosis became global news. It was omnipresent on social media and 1,900 articles were written in a matter of days. 

Many were saddened.

However, joy dominated the commentary. 

People pointed to schadenfreude, the pleasure of another's failure. Yes, there’s that. There is a special place in people’s hearts that loves to see others fail, especially when that person’s presence threatens their own psychological stability in some way or helps them feel better about themselves. 

But, if you look over the social media commentary about me, you’ll see that pattern:

“he deserved it.”

I deserved it because I challenged death. The crowd was running a deeply rooted psychological script that represents the oldest, most deeply embedded stories of human culture. 

This was the first story ever written down, 4,000 years ago. Gilgamesh sought eternal life after losing someone he loved, only to have the plant of youth stolen by a serpent as he bathed. Leaving him to accept his mortality.

Asclepius became so skilled at rejuvenation that he raised the dead. As punishment, Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt to enforce life and death authority.

This is the story of Jesus. Pontius Pilate offered a choice between a thief and the immortalist, and the crowd demanded the execution. 

People need this story conclusion to keep themselves sane. The challenger must lose and the loss must appear deserved. It’s a shield of self preservation.

For if death is inevitable, their existence and that of their loved ones is justified and unavoidable. If death is not inevitable, nothing about their reality is safe. 

I occupy the same philosophical and archetypal position as Gilgamesh, Asclepius and Jesus. 

This statement will draw outrage and accusations of blasphemy, hubris and narcissism. Nevertheless, it’s the pattern that has repeated itself for thousands of years. 

Death has been the omnipresent concern of the human race. It encapsulates our greatest fears, joy and curiosities. The discourse around it changes over time; however, the fundamentals remain unchanged.

What’s different about this moment, that is unlike any other moment, is that physical death may no longer be inevitable.

What if I didn’t deserve it?

And what if I am your ally, and not a threat?

Your brain basically stopped recording your life around age 25. Everything since then is a blur for a reason.

Neuroscientists measured this so many times they named it: the reminiscence bump. Ask anyone over 60 to recall their strongest memories and almost every answer clusters between ages 15 and 25. The decade where everything was new. First job, first apartment, first real relationship. Your brain encoded each day because nothing had a template yet.

After that window closes, most people enter a repetition loop. Same commute, same office, same weekend rhythm. The brain stops recording repeated experiences as distinct events. A year with 300 novel days leaves 300 memory anchors. A year with 10 leaves 10. Both took 365 days to live. Only one of them will exist when you look back.

This is why people at 50 say "where did the time go." The time went into routine that felt like living but left almost nothing behind.

Your remaining years are fixed. How many your brain bothers to remember is entirely up to you.

This has a clinical name. Revenge bedtime procrastination. And the ADHD version runs on a completely different mechanism than the neurotypical one.

A neurotypical person stays up late because they want more leisure time. The ADHD brain stays up because it spent every drop of dopamine it had on executive function during the day. Sitting in meetings, managing transitions, filtering impulses, remembering the thing you were supposed to remember. That burns through dopamine the way sprinting burns through glycogen. By 10pm the tank is empty.

But here's where it gets counterintuitive. The exhaustion is physical. The dopamine deficit is neurological. Those are two separate systems. Your muscles want sleep. Your prefrontal cortex is starving for the stimulation it was denied all day because it spent 14 hours on task-switching and impulse control instead of anything that actually felt rewarding.

The phone at midnight is the brain trying to collect what it's owed. Low-effort, high-stimulation content. Scrolling, short videos, rabbit holes. The exact profile of activity that delivers dopamine without requiring the executive function you already depleted.

The sleep researchers call this a "self-regulation failure." It's closer to a debt collection. You borrowed against your own reward system to function all day. The bill comes due at midnight. And the brain will not let you sleep until it gets paid.
ADHD people being mentally and physically exhausted but still staying up because they didn't get enough "me time" after surviving the whole day.

I've always liked the story of Charlie Munger.

At 31, he was basically at rock bottom.

He was freshly divorced, had lost the house, and his son died of leukemia. Munger paid for every treatment out of pocket and was left with almost nothing.

Yet he kept going.

Instead of drowning in bitterness, he worked, he read, and he kept his head down.

With a new marriage and some stability, he began investing his lawyer's salary into stocks and real estate.

Then in 1959 he met Buffett.

Inspired by someone who was already running his own partnership, Munger founded Wheeler, Munger & Company in 1962.

The wealth started to accumulate. Through real estate projects and his growing investment partnership, Munger became a millionaire around age 43.

Many successful investments followed, many alongside Buffett, and the relationship grew close enough that working together was the only thing that made sense.

Munger wound down his partnership in 1975. Over 13 years, he had compounded at 19.8% annually, against 5% for the Dow.

In 1978, he became Vice Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and helped build the empire it was set to become.

Somewhere along the way he lost an eye to a failed surgery, but that didn't bother him much. He still had one left. Plenty enough to read annual reports.

When most people think of Munger, they just see a rich old wise man who almost stood in Buffett's shadow. But the truth is that Munger's wisdom didn't come from nowhere.

He worked himself up from rock bottom, a place where many others would have stayed down, to become one of the most respected investors in history. And a billionaire on top of that.

He never let it go to his head. He lived in the same house in Pasadena for decades. The place didn't even have AC. He cooled it with ice and fans.

Hard to find a better role model than that.

Game theory explains why forgiving someone who has not paid a cost for betraying you is a vicious mistake dressed up as a virtue. Forgiveness without consequence never 'resets' the relationship. It updates the other person's model of your response function.
You now taught them that betrayal costs nothing. So, the next defection is cheaper than the first one. You have effectively lowered the price of breaking your trust.
Genuine repair requires that the cost of defection be visible and proportional before the relationship resumes. Everything else is an invitation to defection.

I disappeared for 15 days.
No posts.
No designs.

I was in Nepal. And here’s what I realized.

Please read this carefully.

If you're someone struggling to work on new ideas…
If you want real-life experience…
If you truly want to understand what life actually is…

Then please, please, please leave your comfort zone.

I was struggling with the same problems.
I was doing well. Working on client projects. Getting leads. Posting constantly on X.

But I was still missing something.

New ideas.
New experiences.

Now you might ask, why should you listen to me?

Because I was the kind of person who lived in a small town and thought the world was small. I believed I should stay inside my comfort zone.

When you live in a small town or city, you slowly shape your reality based on other people's thoughts and how they judge others.

I was trapped in that same mindset.

And the funny thing is, I’m someone who loves talking to people, listening to their experiences, exploring, and learning new things.

But I was stuck in the same place.

Then one day I told myself, no matter what, I will start visiting new places and open new chapters in my life.

And honestly, this is one of the best decisions I’ve ever made.

In these 15 days, I visited places in Nepal and India.
I learned things no one could ever teach me.

Pure life experience.

When you travel, you meet hundreds of people with different mindsets and different stories. You begin to understand what real life actually is.

It expands your thinking.

One of our devs just turned 23.

He said:
"I feel like I'm too old. I should have learned more in my teenage years."

Almost everyone thinks like that.

Here is some perspective.

I am turning 30 this year.

• Started coding at 11
• First developer agency job at 16
• Then wasted around 8 years in hell

ADHD.
University.
Toxic relationship.
No direction.

At 24 or 25 something clicked.

Self improvement.
Fell in love with software again.
Got obsessed with it.
Hackathons.
Agency jobs.
Fast startup jobs.

Learned everyting about Product. Learned how businesses work.

At 26 I took freelancing seriously.
At 27 I had the idea for FeatherFlow.
At almost 28 it started getting traction and I started hiring.
At 29 I went full time (that was ONE year ago).

Right now?

I earn less than most of my friends with regular jobs.
Almost no savings.
I pay myself as little as possible to reinvest into the company.

We have an INSANELY talented team,

who can make a living doing what they are good at and love.

Sure, I could have been a multimillionaire already if I had not "wasted" those years.

I believe I will be a millionaire within 3 to 4 years.
A multimillionaire within 10.

But even if not,

I am insanely passionate about what I am doing and building.

My life is WONDERFUL even without the big money.

That is the point.

People overestimate what they can do in 1 year.
They underestimate what can happen in 5 to 10 years.

Everything compounds.

You are not too old.

23 is young.
30 is young.
Even 40 or 50 is young.

Stack skills.
Read.
Train your brain.
Build!!
Take ownership!!!

Do that consistently for years.

You will not recognize yourself.

Imagine you're a war strategist.

You’re on the battlefield and you have a limited number of soldiers.

So you need to use these soldiers in the right place.

Because you want to force a breakthrough.

So you concentrate your forces in 1 area.

And you attack at the weakest point.

Because this gives you the best chance to force a breakthrough.

And this applies perfectly to getting things done.

Many people think it’s best to do as much as possible.

But the counterintuitive thing is that you actually get more done by doing less.

Or more precisely - doing less better.

Just like an army, you have a limited amount of attacking power.

So the more problems you attack, the less strength you have for each of them.

So if you want to get a lot done, it’s best to focus on the highest leverage activity.

In other words: you need to attack your problems at their weakest point to get the most done.

And you can only do this if you concentrate your forces.

So doing a lot may feel productive.

But using all your forces for 1 problem is actually the more productive move.

You don't need to do more.

You need to optimize less.

Attack your biggest problem at its weakest point.

That's how you get the most done.
